question: Explain three different types of conformity, using examples.
key_points: Compliance: conforming publicly while privately keeping your own view
An example of compliance, such as laughing at a joke you don't find funny
Identification: conforming publicly and privately while in the group; often temporary
An example of identification, such as recycling only with flatmates
Internalisation: conforming publicly and privately, even when no longer in the group
An example of internalisation, such as remaining vegetarian after leaving a job
source: Conformity and Obedience past paper questions; Lesson 4

question: Explain the two motivations to conform with reference to studies.
key_points: Normative influence: wanting to be liked and accepted by the group
Asch: participants conformed to avoid ridicule when the answer was obvious
People may not agree privately
Normative influence is linked to compliance
Informational influence: wanting to be correct and fear of looking unintelligent
Jenness: participants were unsure and changed their answer towards the group's
Informational influence is linked to internalisation
model_answer:
People conform due to normative social influence, as they don't want to be different from the rest of the group and want to be liked and accepted by the group (1). This was illustrated in Asch's study, where participants conformed with the group due to not wanting to be ridiculed when the answer was obvious (1). People might not agree privately and want to be liked and accepted by the group (1). This is heavily linked to compliance, where people change their answers publicly but maintain their private beliefs (1).

People also conform due to informational social influence because they want to be seen to be correct and have the fear of looking unintelligent (1). This is shown in Jenness' study, where participants were unsure of the answer so looked to others' guesses and changed their answer to align with the group answer (1). This is linked to internalisation, as people change their view publicly to match the group as they are unsure, and change it privately as they think others are correct (1).
source: assessment feedback

question: Explain two individual factors that affect conformity.

Names a second factor and its direction, such as self-esteem or age
Explains why, such as not being influenced by how others evaluate them
Gives evidence, such as Santee and Maslach
model_answer:
Women are more conformist than men (1). This may be because women are more concerned with social relationships than men, and more concerned with group harmony, and therefore conform more (1). This conformity is likely to be caused by normative social influence (1). This is linked to Mori and Arai, where females conformed in 4.41 trials whereas men did not conform (1).

People who are younger tend to conform more (1). Evidence shows that people who are 10-14 tend to conform more (1), and do this because they want to be liked and accepted, and sometimes from peer pressure (1).

question: Describe and evaluate Mori and Arai's investigation into conformity.
key_points: Aim: replicate Asch without confederates
104 Japanese students in groups of four
Filter glasses meant one person saw a different image
Minority participant answered third, aloud
Females conformed on 4.41/12 critical trials; men did not conform
Strength: both genders, so results generalise to males and females
Strength: no confederates, so no acting
Strength: participants knew each other, as in real life
Weakness: Japan only, so not generalisable to other cultures
Weakness: artificial lab setting and deception
source: Mori and Arai higher; Conformity and Obedience past paper questions

question: Analyse Mori and Arai's investigation into conformity.
key_points: 3 descriptive points from aim, method and findings
3 evaluation points, each explained
Link to normative social influence
Conclusion about acquainted people and external validity
Compare with Asch: both found conformity
Contrast with Asch: males did not conform, with a generational explanation
Contrast with Perrin and Spencer
Real-life application, such as bullying or peer pressure
model_answer:
Mori and Arai (2010) carried out an experiment which aimed to replicate Asch's study without the need for confederates. (1) It was carried out as a lab experiment on 104 Japanese male and female student participants who were split into groups of four. (1) Participants wore filter glasses where three participants saw the same image and one saw a different image of the length of lines, similar to Asch's experiment. (1) They were asked to answer out loud with the minority participant always answering third. (1) The results showed that female participants conformed on 4.41/12 critical trials and men did not conform at all. (1)

One strength of Mori and Arai's study is that they used both males and females. (1) This demonstrates that the results can be generalised to both males and females. (1) A weakness is that they only used participants from Japan. (1) Japan is a collectivist culture and conformity levels will be different from individualist cultures, meaning it is not generalisable. (1)

Mori and Arai's study can be supported by normative social influence. Participants were sure of what the answer was as the task was easy, so they went along with it to fit in with the group. (1)

One conclusion is that participants knew each other, unlike in Asch's study. This suggests it is more externally valid, as in real life conformity tends to occur among acquainted people. (1)

Mori and Arai's study contrasts with Asch, as Asch found males conformed on 1/3 of all critical trials and Mori and Arai found that males did not conform at all. (1) This implies that the change in conformity levels could be a result of generational changes in the 55 years since Asch's study. (1)
source: Example Mori and Arai Analysis; assessment feedback

question: Describe Milgram's study of Obedience.
key_points: Aim: whether ordinary people would obey an authority figure when asked to inflict pain
40 American men, told it was a memory and learning study
Mr Wallace was a confederate, always the learner
Shocks rose from 15 to 450 volts for each wrong answer, with prods used

question: Evaluate Milgram's (1963) study of obedience.
hint: Just strengths and weaknesses. A weakness is... This is a weakness because...
key_points: Unethical: participants were deceived about the true aim, so may have acted abnormally
Participants were stressed and not protected from harm
Lacked ecological validity: electric shocks are not an everyday situation
Males only, so cannot be generalised to females
Standardised procedure with prods made it reliable
Each point is explained with "this is a weakness/strength because"
model_answer:
A weakness of Milgram's research is that it was unethical as participants thought they were taking part in a study about memory, not obedience (1). This is a weakness because participants were deceived and could have potentially acted in an abnormal way as a result, therefore results are unreliable (1).

The study lacked ecological validity as it was conducted in a laboratory (1). This is a weakness because it is not something that participants would have to encounter every day, like electric shocks, and they may therefore act differently to what they would in a natural setting (1).

Milgram's sample consisted of males only (1), which means we are unable to generalise the results to females (1).
source: Analyse Milgram

question: Analyse Milgram's study of Obedience.
hint: SLICE. Half your marks must come from analysis.
key_points: Summary of aim, method and results
Evaluation points, each explained
Link to agentic and autonomous states
Link to factors such as proximity and uniform, with why they change obedience
Application: German soldiers following orders in the Second World War
Compare with Bickman: both support uniform; lab versus field
Compare with Hofling: 95% obedience, higher ecological validity
Compare with Burger or Rank and Jacobson
model_answer:
The aim of the study was to see how far ordinary people would go in obeying an authority figure. (1) Milgram recruited 40 volunteers by advertising for a memory and learning experiment. (1) An experimenter introduced each participant to 'Mr Wallace', who they were told was another participant but was actually a confederate working for Milgram. (1) The generator went from 15 to 450 volts and the voltage must be increased for every wrong answer, which the learner purposefully gave. (1) 26 out of 40 (65%) continued up to the max shock level of 450 volts. (1)

A weakness of Milgram's research is that it was unethical, as participants thought they were taking part in a study about memory, not obedience. (1) This is a weakness because participants were deceived and could have acted in an abnormal way as a result, therefore results are unreliable. (1)

It can be concluded that people are in an agentic state when they follow orders given by an authority figure. (1) Participants who did not obey orders took personal responsibility for their actions and so were in an autonomous state. (1)

The results can help us to understand German soldiers' behaviour in the Second World War, as most of the soldiers said that they were following orders given by a higher authority. (1)

Both Milgram and Bickman used experimentation to study obedience, but Milgram's study was carried out in a laboratory whereas Bickman's was in the field, which means that Milgram's study has greater reliability and Bickman's has greater ecological validity. (1) Both studies found that uniform played a part in the levels of obedience. (1)
source: Analyse Milgram; Lesson 2 Milgram

model_answer: If it is a place that is deemed less prestigious, obedience rates are likely to drop (1). This is due to thinking prestigious locations are more credible and being less likely to challenge the authority figure (1). This is shown in a Milgram variation where he gave out orders in a run-down office block compared to the prestigious location of Yale (1) and obedience rates dropped to 47.5% from 65% (1).

scenario: During exam time, a group of school pupils were revising in a classroom, supervised by a teacher. A pair of the pupils started chatting to one another. After a short while, they were told by the teacher that they must not talk, and they immediately stopped and returned to their work. A short while later, the teacher got up and left the room, and the pair of pupils began to talk to each other again. A fellow pupil told them to be quiet, saying that they were disturbing others who wanted to revise. However, this time the pair didn't obey the command, and continued to chat.
question: Explain the scenario above with reference to two or more factors that can affect obedience.
key_points: The pupils obey the teacher when present, but leaving creates a buffer that reduces authority
Milgram: obedience dropped from 65% when the experimenter gave instructions by phone
The teacher is a legitimate authority
Children learn from a young age to follow a teacher's instructions (socialisation)
The teacher has the power to apply sanctions
A peer is not a legitimate authority figure
A teacher has institutional or legal power, and expert power
A charismatic pupil with high social status might have been obeyed
model_answer:
The pupils obey the authority figure when they are there, (1) but when they leave the room, there is a buffer that makes their authority less powerful. (1) This is similar to the work of Milgram, who found that obedience dropped from 65% when the experimenter left the room and gave instructions by phone. (1)

Here, the teacher is a legitimate authority, (1) because children learn from a young age that they are expected to follow a teacher's instructions (1) and also because the teacher has the power to apply sanctions. (1) However, peers are not legitimate authorities, and obedience involves getting a direct command from someone of a higher social status or level of power. (1)

A teacher has institutional/legal power over a pupil, (1) as they have the ability to inflict punishments. (1) Teachers are also obeyed because of their expert power. (1) If the fellow pupil had been a highly charismatic personality with high social status, the pair of pupils may have obeyed. (1)
source: lesson 8 - Mori and Arai (marking instructions)

scenario: Sam is a security guard. Sam's supervisor has ordered her to give a disciplinary warning to another security guard for lateness. Sam tells her supervisor she feels uncomfortable with this, but Sam's supervisor insists that she must. Sam refuses to obey.
question: Explain three or more factors that affect obedience, with reference to the above scenario. You should refer to research evidence in your answer.
hint: Use statistics and examples from Milgram. Always read the scenario fully.
key_points: Factor 1, for example location, with the direction of the effect
Explanation linked to Sam, for example challenging the supervisor's right to give orders
Milgram's variation with statistics, for example 47.5% from 65%
Factor 2: agency theory, with Sam taking responsibility in an autonomous state
Milgram: 35% remained autonomous, 65% went to 450 volts
Factor 3, for example uniform or proximity, with evidence
Every point is linked back to Sam
model_answer:
Location is another factor that is impacting Sam's obedience. If it is a place that is deemed less prestigious, obedience rates are likely to drop (1). This is due to challenging the authority figure and thinking 'have they the right to tell me what to do?' (1). This is shown in Sam's case, where they might not have obeyed due to it being a less prestigious, run-down location, which challenges the supervisor's authority. This is shown in a Milgram variation where he gave out orders in a run-down office block compared to the prestigious location of Yale (1), and obedience rates dropped to 47.5% from 65%. (1)

Sam takes responsibility for their behaviour, which reduces obedience (1). Someone in an agentic state is acting on behalf of the authority figure so they pass over responsibility for their behaviour to the authority figure (1), which increases obedience (1). The process by which people move from autonomous behaviour to agentic behaviour is known as agentic shift (1).

In the scenario, the authority figure (the supervisor) tries to put Sam into an agentic state by giving her a direct order (1). This would remove the responsibility for Sam's actions from her (1). Sam, however, stays independent from the authority figure's orders by refusing to obey (1). She remains in an autonomous state by not giving the warning (1). Sam's behaviour reflects Milgram's findings that 35% of his participants remained autonomous (1).
source: assessment feedback
